english: it's not that simple; not so fast
use: Push back when someone suggests an easy way out or tries to get away with something.

example.romaji: yasumitai kedo, sou wa ikanai n da yo.
example.ja: 休みたいけど、そうはいかないんだよ。
example.english: I'd love a day off, but it's not that simple.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumitai n desu kedo, sou wa ikanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 休みたいんですけど、そうはいかないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'd love a day off, but it's not that simple.

notes: iku here means 'go smoothly', as in umaku ikanai (it isn't going well).

use: Soft opener before you tell someone something; common with kids and partners.

example.romaji: ano ne, kyou gakkou de omoshiroi koto atta no.
example.ja: あのね、今日学校で面白いことあったの。
example.english: You know what? Something funny happened at school today.

notes: ano alone is a hesitant 'um'; ano ne and ano sa announce you have something to say.

use: Casual opener before a question or news among friends; more direct than ano ne.

example.romaji: ano sa, ashita hima? eiga ikanai?
example.ja: あのさ、明日暇？映画行かない？
example.english: Hey, are you free tomorrow? Want to see a movie?

notes: With people you'd speak politely to, open with ano, sumimasen instead.

politeJa: ちょっと聞いてください
english: listen to this; hear me out
use: Grab a friend's attention before news or a rant; chotto kiite yo is more insistent.

example.romaji: chotto kiite! kinou sugoi koto ga atta no.
example.ja: ちょっと聞いて！昨日すごいことがあったの。
example.english: Listen to this! Something crazy happened yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kiite kudasai. kinou sugoi koto ga atta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと聞いてください。昨日すごいことがあったんです。
examplePolite.english: Listen to this. Something amazing happened yesterday.

notes: kiku also means 'ask': chotto kiite ii? is 'can I ask you something?'

use: Call to someone far off or not paying attention; also 'anyone there?'

example.romaji: ooi, kotchi da yo! hayaku oide!
example.ja: おーい、こっちだよ！早くおいで！
example.english: Hey, over here! Come on!

notes: To get a stranger's attention, say sumimasen instead.

english: let's see; let me have a look
use: Said as you lean in to look at something someone wants to show you.

example.romaji: dore dore, chotto misete.
example.ja: どれどれ、ちょっと見せて。
example.english: Let's see, show me.

examplePolite.ja: どれどれ、ちょっと見せてください。
examplePolite.english: Let's see, may I have a look?

notes: Sounds a little like a parent or teacher checking something.

english: I didn't know (that); I had no idea
use: React to news or a fact that surprises you, often after e, honto?

example.romaji: e, kekkon shita no? zenzen shiranakatta!
example.ja: え、結婚したの？全然知らなかった！
example.english: What, you got married? I had no idea!

examplePolite.romaji: e, kekkon sareta n desu ka? zenzen shirimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: え、結婚されたんですか？全然知りませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Oh, you got married? I had no idea.

notes: shiranai (present) is 'I don't know'; use the past for news you've just heard.

english: oh, so that's it; now I get it
use: Said when something finally makes sense, often half to yourself.

example.romaji: aa, sou iu koto ka! yatto wakatta.
example.ja: ああ、そういうことか！やっと分かった。
example.english: Oh, so that's it! I finally get it.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, sou iu koto desu ne. yatto wakarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、そういうことですね。やっと分かりました。
examplePolite.english: Ah, so that's what it is. Now I understand.

notes: Close to naruhodo; the ka falls, so it isn't a question.

english: I didn't notice; I didn't realize
use: When you missed something right in front of you; also an apology for an oversight.

example.romaji: gomen, kiteta no? zenzen kizukanakatta.
example.ja: ごめん、来てたの？全然気づかなかった。
example.english: Sorry, you were here? I didn't notice at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, irasshatta n desu ka. zenzen kizukimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、いらっしゃったんですか。全然気づきませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, you were here? I didn't notice at all.

notes: shiranakatta is for facts you didn't know; kizukanakatta is for things you failed to see.

use: Shout for help in danger; to a friend it can also be a jokey 'help me out'.

example.romaji: dareka tasukete! hito ga taoreta!
example.ja: 誰か助けて！人が倒れた！
example.english: Somebody help! Someone's collapsed!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tasukete kudasai! hito ga taoremashita!
examplePolite.ja: すみません、助けてください！人が倒れました！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please help! Someone's collapsed!

notes: For everyday help with a task, tetsudatte (give me a hand) is more natural.

kana: きゅうきゅうしゃをよんで
politeJa: 救急車を呼んでください
use: Ask a bystander to call; the number in Japan is 119, which also reaches the fire service.

example.romaji: hayaku kyuukyuusha o yonde! ishiki ga nai.
example.ja: 早く救急車を呼んで！意識がない。
example.english: Quick, call an ambulance! She's unconscious.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、救急車を呼んでください！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please call an ambulance!

notes: Police is 110 (keisatsu); 119 is ambulance and fire.

use: Shouted when the shaking starts; announcements and teachers use jishin desu.

example.romaji: a, jishin da! hayaku tsukue no shita ni!
example.ja: あっ、地震だ！早く机の下に！
example.english: Whoa, earthquake! Quick, under the table!

examplePolite.romaji: jishin desu! tsukue no shita ni haitte kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: 地震です！机の下に入ってください！

notes: The early-warning alert on phones and TV says jishin desu, jishin desu.

use: Point and say it at a clinic or pharmacy; the doctor asks doko ga itai desu ka? (where does it hurt?).

example.romaji: kinou kara koko ga itai n da.
example.ja: 昨日からここが痛いんだ。
example.english: It's been hurting here since yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara koko ga itai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日からここが痛いんです。
examplePolite.english: It's been hurting here since yesterday.

notes: itai! alone is 'ouch!'; swap koko for a body part: atama ga itai (my head hurts).

english: where am I?; where is this?
use: Muttered on waking up somewhere strange or getting lost; ask strangers with the polite form.

example.romaji: are, koko doko? machigaeta kamo.
example.ja: あれ、ここどこ？間違えたかも。
example.english: Huh, where am I? I might've gone the wrong way.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, koko wa doko desu ka? chizu de oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ここはどこですか？地図で教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, where is this? Could you show me on the map?

use: Tell a passer-by or a friend on the phone that you don't know where you are.

example.romaji: gomen, michi ni mayotta. chotto okureru.
example.ja: ごめん、道に迷った。ちょっと遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I got lost. I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, michi ni mayotte shimatte, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、道に迷ってしまって、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I got lost, so I'll be a little late.

notes: mayou alone also means 'can't decide': dotchi ni suru ka mayotteru.

src: どう行けばいいですか
ja: どう行けばいいですか
kana: どういけばいいですか
use: Ask a stranger or staff for directions after naming the place: X made dou ikeba ii desu ka?

example.romaji: sumimasen, eki made dou ikeba ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、駅までどう行けばいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

notes: With friends: dou ikeba ii? Simpler still: eki wa doko desu ka? (where's the station?).

use: A common late-night problem: trains stop around midnight, leaving a taxi, a net cafe or a long walk.

example.romaji: yabai, shuuden nogashita. takushii shika nai.
example.ja: やばい、終電逃した。タクシーしかない。
example.english: Crap, I missed the last train. It's a taxi now.

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden o nogashita node, takushii de kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 終電を逃したので、タクシーで帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I missed the last train, so I'll take a taxi home.

notes: shuuden is the last train; the first one of the day is shihatsu.

use: Say a thing has broken or stopped working.

example.romaji: aa, sumaho kowareta. gamen ga tsukanai.
example.ja: ああ、スマホ壊れた。画面がつかない。
example.english: Ugh, my phone's broken. The screen won't turn on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho ga kowaremashita. gamen ga tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: スマホが壊れました。画面がつきません。
examplePolite.english: My phone broke. The screen won't turn on.

english: it won't work; it won't move; it's stuck
use: For machines that won't run, doors or lids that won't budge, or a body part you can't move.

example.romaji: kono kopiiki, mata ugokanai yo.
example.ja: このコピー機、また動かないよ。
example.english: This copier's not working again.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kono kopiiki ga ugokanai n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、このコピー機が動かないんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, this copier isn't working.

notes: For screens and lights that won't come on, use tsukanai.

english: I left something behind; I forgot something
use: When you realize you left something at home, on a train or in a shop.

example.romaji: a, wasuremono shita! chotto modoru ne.
example.ja: あ、忘れ物した！ちょっと戻るね。
example.english: Oh, I forgot something! I'll run back.

examplePolite.romaji: a, wasuremono o shimashita. chotto modorimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、忘れ物をしました。ちょっと戻ります。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I left something behind. I'll just go back.

notes: On trains you'll hear owasuremono in announcements reminding you not to leave things behind.
